category: VSM peripheral and device model library
description: The embedded peripheral models that ship with every Proteus VSM family licence and the general simulation libraries: character and graphical LCDs, TFT/OLED panels, LED drivers and seven-segment displays, keypads, switches and potentiometers, memories and storage cards, real-time clocks, temperature/humidity/pressure/light sensors, motors and their drivers, communication devices (RS-232, COMPIM, CAN, Ethernet, USB-serial, port expanders), ADC/DAC converters, analogue ICs, logic families, regulators and discrete primitives. Names are the library part names used in the Pick Devices dialog where known.

tools.name: LM016L (HD44780 16x2 LCD)
tools.description: The standard animated character LCD model: an HD44780-compatible 16-character, 2-line alphanumeric display with the usual RS/RW/E control pins and D0-D7 data bus, supporting 4-bit and 8-bit interfaces, the full instruction set (clear, home, entry mode, display/cursor control, shift, function set, CGRAM custom characters) and busy-flag polling. It is the model most tutorials use for LCD firmware on PIC, AVR, 8051 and ARM.
tools.usage: Pick Devices > keyword 'LM016L' (DISPLAY.LIB) > wire RS/RW/E and D4-D7 (4-bit) or D0-D7 (8-bit) to the MCU; VSS/VDD/VEE are implicit

parameters.name: Interface width
parameters.description: Determined by the firmware's Function Set command (4- or 8-bit).

parameters.name: Contrast pin (VEE)
parameters.description: Modelled as a pin but the display renders regardless of contrast voltage.

tools.example: PIC16F877A PORTD to LM016L D4-D7, RD0=RS, RD1=E, RW tied to ground; run 'Hello World' firmware and the text appears on the animated glass.
tools.notes: Timing violations (writing before the busy flag clears) are reported in the Simulation Log rather than silently ignored. Related models: LM017L, LM018L, LM020L (16x1), LM032L (20x2), LM041L (16x4), LM044L (20x4), Milford 16x2/20x2/40x2/20x4.

tools.name: LM044L / LM041L / LM032L / LM020L (HD44780 LCD variants)
tools.description: The other HD44780-controller character displays in DISPLAY.LIB: LM020L (16x1), LM032L (20x2), LM041L (16x4), LM044L (20x4), plus LM017L/LM018L and the Milford 16x2, 20x2, 40x2 and 20x4 panels. They share the LM016L pinout and command set, differing only in DDRAM line addressing (0x00/0x40/0x14/0x54 for four-line parts), so a firmware LCD driver can be validated against each glass size.
tools.usage: Pick Devices > 'LM044L' etc.; same wiring as LM016L

parameters.name: Line addresses
parameters.description: Row start addresses differ per size; four-line models use 0x00, 0x40, 0x14, 0x54.

tools.example: Swap LM016L for LM044L in a menu-driven design to check that the firmware's line-3/line-4 addressing is correct.
tools.notes: All are HD44780-parallel; use JHD-2X16-I2C for an I2C backpack display.

tools.name: JHD-2X16-I2C (I2C character LCD)
tools.description: A 16x2 character LCD with an on-board I2C interface, used to simulate 'I2C backpack' style displays driven from an MCU's TWI/MSSP/Wire bus with only SDA and SCL. It lets LiquidCrystal_I2C-style Arduino libraries and PIC/AVR I2C LCD drivers be tested including address selection and the ACK/NACK sequence visible on the I2C Protocol Analyser.
tools.usage: Pick Devices > 'JHD-2X16-I2C' > SDA/SCL to the MCU bus with pull-ups; set the slave address to match the firmware

parameters.name: I2C address
parameters.description: Device property matching the address the firmware writes to.

tools.example: Arduino Uno + JHD-2X16-I2C: LiquidCrystal_I2C lcd(0x27,16,2); lcd.print("Ready"); the text renders and the analyser shows the address byte 0x4E.
tools.notes: Many PCF8574-based backpacks map pins differently; adjust the library's pin mapping rather than the model.

tools.name: Graphical LCD modules (LM3228/LM4228 T6963C, PG12864F/PG24064F/PG128128A/PG160128A KS0108 class)
tools.description: Monochrome graphic LCD models with embedded controllers: the LM3228, LM3229, LM3267, LM3283, LM3287, LM4228, LM4229, LM4265, LM4267, LM4283 and LM4287 (Toshiba T6963C-style text/graphics controllers at 240x64 to 320x240) and the Powertip PG12864F (128x64, KS0108 dual-controller), PG24064F (240x64), PG128128A and PG160128A. They render pixel data written through the parallel command/data interface so GLCD drivers (u8g2/KS0108/T6963C libraries) can be debugged visually.
tools.usage: Pick Devices > 'PG12864F' or 'LM4228' > wire the 8-bit data bus and control lines (CS1/CS2, RS, R/W, E for KS0108; WR/RD/CE/CD for T6963C)

parameters.name: Controller type
parameters.description: Fixed per part: KS0108 (PG12864F, dual chip select) or T6963C (LMxxxx).

tools.example: AVR ATmega32 + PG12864F: run a KS0108 driver that draws a sine wave; pixels appear column by column as the firmware writes pages.
tools.notes: Other KS0108 128x64 modules (e.g. LGM12641BS1R, AMPIRE128X64) also exist in the display library. For serial/SPI displays use PCD8544 (Nokia), UC1701 or the OLED models.

tools.name: Nokia 3310 / 5110 / 7110 LCD (PCD8544)
tools.description: Models of the Nokia phone displays widely used in hobby projects: the 84x48 Nokia 3310 and 5110 glass driven by the Philips PCD8544 controller over a 3-wire SPI-style serial link (SCLK, DIN, D/C, SCE, RST), and the larger Nokia 7110 (SED1565-type) module. Contrast, bias and inverse-video commands are honoured, so Adafruit_PCD8544/u8g2 drivers can be checked pixel for pixel.
tools.usage: Pick Devices > 'NOKIA 5110' / 'PCD8544' > SCLK, DIN, DC, SCE, RST to MCU pins; LED backlight pin optional

parameters.name: Serial interface
parameters.description: Write-only SPI mode 0, MSB first; the model decodes command vs data from the D/C pin.

tools.example: Arduino Nano + Nokia 5110 breakout from the Visual Designer gallery: drawText() methods render on the 84x48 panel in the simulation.
tools.notes: The 5110 breakout board is also available as a Visual Designer peripheral with high-level draw methods.

tools.name: ILI9341 320x240 TFT LCD
tools.description: A colour TFT model built on the ILI9341 controller (320x240, 16-bit RGB565) with an SPI interface and backlight pin, matching the Adafruit 2.8" TFT shield/breakout and generic '2.4 TFT SPI' modules. It executes the ILI9341 command set (memory write with column/page address windows, rotation via MADCTL, pixel format, display on/off) so graphics libraries such as Adafruit_ILI9341/TFT_eSPI render exactly as on hardware.
tools.usage: Pick Devices > 'ILI9341' > SCK/MOSI/MISO, CS, D/C, RST to the MCU SPI pins; or add the Adafruit TFT shield peripheral in Visual Designer

parameters.name: SPI mode
parameters.description: Mode 0, up to the MCU's SPI clock; the model is transaction-accurate.

parameters.name: Backlight
parameters.description: LED pin controls the rendered backlight state.

tools.example: Uno + Adafruit TFT shield with an SD resource: drawBitmap() streams a BMP from the simulated SD card onto the ILI9341 panel; breakpoint inside drawBitmap() to watch SPI traffic.
tools.notes: Rendering a full frame over SPI is slow in simulation (millions of transactions); reduce the animation frame rate or draw partial regions while debugging.

tools.name: OLED12864I2C / OLED12832I2C (SSD1306 OLED)
tools.description: 128x64 and 128x32 monochrome OLED models based on the Solomon SSD1306 controller with an I2C interface (address 0x3C/0x3D). Page addressing, horizontal/vertical addressing modes, contrast, display inversion and charge-pump commands are modelled, so Adafruit_SSD1306, u8g2 and MicroPython ssd1306 drivers can be verified on PIC, AVR, ARM, Arduino and Pico targets.
tools.usage: Pick Devices > 'OLED12864I2C' > SDA/SCL to the MCU with pull-ups; set the I2C address property if the firmware uses 0x3D

parameters.name: I2C address
parameters.description: 0x3C default (0x78 write); switch to 0x3D for modules with the alternate strap.

tools.example: Pico W (MicroPython) + OLED12864I2C: ssd1306.SSD1306_I2C(128,64,i2c).text('Temp 24C',0,0); show() renders on the OLED.
tools.notes: An SPI-interface SSD1306 model is not listed on the peripherals page; use the I2C parts or UC1701 for SPI. Also see the Grove OLED module in the Visual Designer gallery.

tools.name: UC1701 and EA DOGS102N-6 (SPI graphic LCDs)
tools.description: Small SPI-driven monochrome graphic LCD controllers: the UC1701 (128x64, ST7565-compatible command set used in many 'COG 12864' modules) and the Electronic Assembly EA DOGS102N-6 (102x64 DOG-series display). Both render page-mapped pixel data written over a 4-wire SPI with a command/data select pin.
tools.usage: Pick Devices > 'UC1701' / 'EA DOGS102N-6' > SCK, MOSI, CS0, CD/A0, RST

parameters.name: Interface
parameters.description: SPI write-only; the model decodes ST7565-class commands (page/column set, display start line, contrast).

tools.example: STM32F103 + UC1701 with a u8g2 ST7565 constructor; verify the initialisation sequence with the SPI Protocol Analyser.
tools.notes: Choose these when the target hardware uses an ST7565/UC1701 glass rather than the KS0108 parallel modules.

tools.name: 7-segment displays (7SEG-COM-CATHODE, 7SEG-COM-ANODE, 7SEG-MPX4-CC, 7SEG-BCD)
tools.description: Animated seven-segment display models in DISPLAY.LIB: single digits with common cathode or common anode (7SEG-COM-CATHODE / 7SEG-COM-ANODE, also in red/green/blue colours), multiplexed 2/4/6/8-digit blocks (7SEG-MPX2-CC/CA, 7SEG-MPX4-CC/CA, 7SEG-MPX6, 7SEG-MPX8) with a common pin per digit for scanning firmware, and 7SEG-BCD which decodes a 4-bit BCD input directly for quick logic experiments.
tools.usage: Pick Devices > '7SEG-MPX4-CC' > segment pins a-g(,dp) to a port, digit commons through transistors or directly to select pins

parameters.name: Polarity
parameters.description: CC (common cathode, segment high = on) or CA (common anode).

parameters.name: Digits
parameters.description: 1, 2, 4, 6 or 8 multiplexed digits.

tools.example: 8051 counting 0000-9999 on 7SEG-MPX4-CC with a 1kHz scan; pause the simulation and the display shows only the digit currently driven - expected for a multiplexed model.
tools.notes: Because the model is time-accurate, a paused/single-stepped display shows only one active digit. Use MAX7219 or TM1637 driver models for serially driven displays.

tools.name: LED driver ICs (MAX7219, TM1637, MAX6950-MAX6955, PCA9685, MY9221, P9813)
tools.description: Serial display/LED driver models: MAX7219 (SPI, 8 digits or 8x8 matrix, cascadable), TM1637 (2-wire 4-digit clock display driver), the MAX6950-MAX6955 SPI/I2C LED display drivers, PCA9685 (I2C 16-channel 12-bit PWM, the Adafruit servo/PWM driver), and the MY9221 and P9813 chained RGB LED drivers used by Grove LED bars and Chainable RGB LEDs. Each decodes its protocol and drives attached LED/segment/servo models.
tools.usage: Pick Devices > 'MAX7219' > DIN/CLK/LOAD from the MCU, segment/digit outputs to a 7SEG-MPX8 or an 8x8 matrix; 'PCA9685' > SDA/SCL, PWM outputs to MOTOR-PWMSERVO

parameters.name: Protocol
parameters.description: SPI (MAX7219/MAX695x), I2C (PCA9685, MAX6953/6955) or proprietary 2-wire (TM1637).

tools.example: Arduino + MAX7219 + 8x8 LED matrix: LedControl library scrolls text; the matrix animates and the SPI analyser shows the 16-bit address/data frames.
tools.notes: PCA9685 pairs with the Adafruit 16-channel PWM/Servo shield in the Visual Designer gallery.

tools.name: LEDs, bargraphs and lamps (LED-RED, LED-BIRG, LED-BARGRAPH-RED, RGBLED, LAMP)
tools.description: Animated indicator models: single LEDs in red/green/yellow/blue/white (LED-RED etc.) with a forward-voltage/current model that lights when current flows, bi-colour LEDs (LED-BIRG, LED-BIBY), 10-segment bargraphs (LED-BARGRAPH-RED/GRN), RGB LED (common anode/cathode) and incandescent LAMP models whose brightness follows power dissipation. Wire-colour animation also shows the logic state on the driving pin.
tools.usage: Pick Devices > 'LED-RED' > anode to the driving pin via a series resistor, cathode to ground

parameters.name: Model type
parameters.description: Analogue (SPICE diode) or digital primitive - the ACTIVE library LEDs are analogue and need a current-limiting resistor.

parameters.name: Colour
parameters.description: Chosen by part name; RGBLED takes three current inputs.

tools.example: Blink demo: PIC RB0 > 330R > LED-RED; if the LED never lights, check the Simulation Log for 'excessive current' or a missing ground.
tools.notes: LEDs driven directly with no resistor trigger a warning (current not limited) and may not animate. LED-BARGRAPH parts are used for VU meters and port monitors.

tools.name: Keypads (KEYPAD-PHONE, KEYPAD-SMALLCALC, KEYPAD-CALCULATOR)
tools.description: Interactive matrix keypad models in ACTIVE.LIB: KEYPAD-PHONE (3x4 telephone layout 0-9,*,#), KEYPAD-SMALLCALC (4x4 hexadecimal/calculator) and KEYPAD-CALCULATOR (larger calculator layout). Row and column pins form a true switch matrix, so row-scan/column-read firmware, debouncing and ghosting behaviour are exercised exactly as on hardware; keys are pressed by clicking them during simulation.
tools.usage: Pick Devices > 'KEYPAD-PHONE' > rows A-D to output pins, columns 1-3/4 to input pins with pull-ups

parameters.name: Matrix size
parameters.description: 3x4 (phone) or 4x4 (small calculator).

tools.example: PIC16F887 PORTB keypad scan with internal pull-ups: click '5' during simulation and the decoded digit is written to the LM016L.
tools.notes: Keys are momentary; hold the mouse button for long-press tests. Also available as Grove/breakout keypad peripherals in Visual Designer.

tools.name: Switches and push buttons (BUTTON, SW-SPST, SW-SPDT, SW-ROT-3, DIPSW_4)
tools.description: Interactive mechanical input models: BUTTON (momentary push button, clicked or latched with the small arrow), SW-SPST/SW-SPDT toggle switches, SW-ROT-3/SW-ROT-6 rotary selectors, DIPSW_x DIP-switch banks and SW-DPDT. They are ideal switches with no bounce by default, which makes them useful for logic tests but means debounce code must be tested with a real-time breakpoint or a pulse generator producing bounce.
tools.usage: Pick Devices > 'BUTTON' > one side to the input pin (with pull-up), other side to ground; click during simulation

parameters.name: Latching
parameters.description: BUTTON is momentary; the arrow control toggles a latched state for hands-free testing.

tools.example: Mode-select button on RD2 with a pull-up; in the Getting Started firmware each click cycles time > temperature > POT display.
tools.notes: Contact bounce is not modelled; use a DPattern generator with a bouncy pattern to test debouncing.

tools.name: Potentiometers (POT-HG, POT-LIN, POT-LOG)
tools.description: Interactive potentiometer models whose wiper is moved with on-screen up/down actuators during simulation: POT-HG (high granularity, fine steps - the usual choice for ADC input testing), POT-LIN (linear taper) and POT-LOG (logarithmic/audio taper). The resistance value and the wiper position are properties, and the wiper voltage feeds ADC channels, comparators or op-amp circuits.
tools.usage: Pick Devices > 'POT-HG' > ends to VDD/GND, wiper to the ADC pin; click the +/- arrows while running

parameters.name: Value
parameters.description: Total resistance (e.g. 10k).

parameters.name: Granularity
parameters.description: POT-HG steps in 1% increments; POT-LIN/LOG in coarser steps.

tools.example: Sweep POT-HG on AN0 while watching ADRESH:ADRESL in the Watch Window reach 0x3FF at full scale.
tools.notes: Digital potentiometer ICs (MCP41xx, AD52xx, DS1804) are separate SPI/I2C models.

tools.name: Digital potentiometers (MCP4131-MCP4262, AD5204/AD5206/AD5220/AD5241/AD5242, DS1804, DS1867, MAX5408-MAX5411)
tools.description: SPI and I2C digital potentiometer models: Microchip MCP4131-MCP4152 and MCP4141-MCP4262 (SPI, 7/8-bit, single/dual, volatile and non-volatile), MCP4017-MCP4019 (I2C), Analog Devices AD5204/AD5206 (SPI multi-channel), AD5220 (up/down), AD5241/AD5242 (I2C), Dallas DS1804 (up/down/increment), DS1867/DS1881, and Maxim MAX5408-MAX5411 audio pots. The wiper resistance changes as the firmware writes, so digitally controlled gain, filter cut-off and volume circuits can be swept from code.
tools.usage: Pick Devices > 'MCP4131' > SCK/SDI/CS from the MCU, PA0/PW0/PB0 in the analogue path

parameters.name: Resolution / taps
parameters.description: 129 (7-bit) or 257 (8-bit) positions depending on the part.

tools.example: MCP4131 as the feedback resistor of a non-inverting op-amp; write 0x40 then 0x7F and see the gain step on the oscilloscope.
tools.notes: Non-volatile parts retain the wiper across simulation runs only if 'Reset Persistent Model Data' has not been invoked.

tools.name: Sounders and speakers (SOUNDER, SPEAKER, BUZZER)
tools.description: Audio output models: SOUNDER (piezo/active sounder that plays the driven frequency through the PC sound card), SPEAKER (loudspeaker with impedance property that renders the analogue waveform as audio) and BUZZER (fixed-tone DC buzzer that sounds when powered). They give audible feedback for tone-generation, alarm and audio-playback firmware and are the sinks for the Audio generator/graph workflow.
tools.usage: Pick Devices > 'SOUNDER' > one pin to the PWM/tone output, other to ground (or through a transistor for SPEAKER)

parameters.name: Impedance / voltage
parameters.description: SPEAKER impedance (8R) and SOUNDER operating voltage properties.

tools.example: Arduino tone(9, 440) on a SOUNDER: the PC plays a 440Hz tone while the simulation runs in real time.
tools.notes: Audio output requires the simulation to keep up with real time; heavy circuits play stuttered audio. Use the Audio graph to analyse the waveform offline instead.

tools.name: I2C EEPROMs (24AA/24LC/24FC series, AT24C, FM24C, M24, ST24)
tools.description: Fully simulated I2C serial EEPROM family in I2CMEM.LIB: Microchip 24AA/24LC/24FC 16-bit and 8-bit address parts (24LC01B up to 24LC1025), Atmel AT24C series, Ramtron FM24C F-RAM, ST M24 and ST24 series. Device address pins A0-A2, write-protect, page writes with page-boundary wrap, acknowledge polling during the write cycle and the internal write time are modelled, and the memory contents can be pre-loaded from a file and inspected in a debug memory window.
tools.usage: Pick Devices > '24LC256' > SDA/SCL with pull-ups, A0-A2 strapped; property 'Initial Contents' file (optional)

parameters.name: A0-A2
parameters.description: Hardware address bits combined with the 1010 device code.

parameters.name: Initial memory contents
parameters.description: Binary/hex file loaded at simulation start; persists between runs unless reset.

tools.example: dsPIC33 data recorder writes samples to a 24LC256; pause and open Debug > 24LC256 memory window to check the stored bytes.
tools.notes: Write-cycle timing (5ms) is enforced - firmware that does not poll for ACK sees NACKs in the I2C analyser. Contents persist across runs (Debug > Reset Persistent Model Data clears them).

tools.name: SPI flash, F-RAM, SRAM and EPROM memories (AT25F, M25PE/M45PE, 23A/23LC, FM25V, 6116/6264/62256, 27C series)
tools.description: Parallel and serial memory models: SPI flash AT25F series and ST M25PE/M45PE (page program, sector erase, status register), Microchip 23A/23LC SPI SRAM, Cypress FM25V SPI F-RAM, parallel SRAM 6116/6164/6264/62256 and PCF8570 (I2C SRAM), parallel EPROM 2764/27128/27256/27512/27C series (loadable from a HEX/BIN file), IDT7203-7208 FIFOs and PCA/74 latches for bus demultiplexing. They let external-memory bus firmware (8051 MOVX, PIC PMP) and SPI file systems be simulated.
tools.usage: Pick Devices > 'M25PE80' > SPI pins; or '62256' on an 8051 address/data bus with a 74HC373 latch; EPROMs take an 'Initial Contents' file property

parameters.name: Initial contents
parameters.description: File loaded into ROM/flash at start (EPROM, flash).

parameters.name: Erase/program timing
parameters.description: Modelled for flash parts; status-register busy bit must be polled.

tools.example: 8051 external RAM test: 62256 + 74HC373; run a MOVX read/write loop and inspect the RAM in its memory debug window.
tools.notes: For SD/MMC cards use the Virtual MMC Card model instead of raw flash.

tools.name: Virtual MMC/SD card (MMC) and ATA/IDE hard disk
tools.description: Storage device models that map a disk-image file on the host PC to a simulated card or drive: the Virtual MMC Card (MMC part) implements the SD/MMC SPI-mode command set (CMD0/CMD8/ACMD41/CMD17/CMD24 etc.) so FatFs, SdFat and Arduino SD library code works against a FAT16/FAT32 image, and the ATA/IDE hard disk model exposes a parallel ATA register interface for embedded file-system experiments. Visual Designer resources (bitmaps, WAV files) are placed on the card image automatically.
tools.usage: Pick Devices > 'MMC' > CS, DI, DO, SCLK to the MCU SPI; property 'Card Image File' = path to a .img (create/size it from the part's context menu)

parameters.name: Card Image File
parameters.description: Host file holding the card contents; must be FAT16/FAT32 formatted for file-system libraries.

parameters.name: Image size
parameters.description: Set large enough for the resources (WAV files need more than bitmaps).

tools.example: Uno + SD breakout (Visual Designer): add logo.bmp as a resource; the wizard writes it into the card image (8.3 filenames) and drawBitmap() reads it back over SPI.
tools.notes: FAT16 requires 8.3 filenames; long names fail silently. The image persists between runs so written log files can be opened on the PC afterwards.

tools.name: Real-time clocks (DS1307, DS1302, DS1338, DS1340, DS3232, DS3234, PCF8583, PCF8593, DS12885/DS12887, MCP79410-MCP79412)
tools.description: RTC models covering I2C (DS1307, DS1338, DS1340 series, DS3232, PCF8583/PCF8593, PC8563, MCP79410-79412), SPI (DS3234) and 3-wire (DS1302) interfaces plus the parallel-bus DS12885/DS12887 PC-clock chips. Time registers advance with simulation time (optionally seeded from the PC clock), alarms, square-wave outputs, battery-backed RAM and the DS3232/3234 temperature-compensated features are modelled, so clock-setting, alarm and calendar firmware is testable without waiting real minutes.
tools.usage: Pick Devices > 'DS1307' > SDA/SCL, SQW/OUT optional; edit the part to set the initial time or use the host clock

parameters.name: Initial time
parameters.description: Property to start from a fixed date/time or the PC's current time.

parameters.name: Square-wave output
parameters.description: SQW frequency selectable by firmware (1Hz, 4.096kHz, 8.192kHz, 32.768kHz on DS1307).

tools.example: PIC + DS1307 + LM016L clock: set 23:59:55 in the model, run, and watch the firmware roll over to 00:00:00 with the date incrementing.
tools.notes: DS3231 is not listed by that name - use DS3232 (same RTC core plus SRAM) for DS3231 firmware. The 32.768kHz crystal drawn on the schematic is not required by the model.

tools.name: 1-Wire thermometers (DS18B20, DS18S20, DS1822, DS1620, DS1621)
tools.description: Dallas/Maxim digital temperature sensors: the 1-Wire DS18B20 (9-12-bit), DS18S20 and DS1822 with ROM search/match, parasite power, conversion timing and scratchpad CRC, plus the DS1620 (3-wire) and DS1621 (I2C) thermostat parts. The temperature is set interactively with on-model buttons during simulation so conversion, CRC checking and multi-drop ROM search code can be exercised.
tools.usage: Pick Devices > 'DS18B20' > DQ to the MCU pin with a 4k7 pull-up; click the +/- buttons to change the sensed temperature while running

parameters.name: Temperature
parameters.description: Interactive value shown on the part; resolution set by the configuration register.

parameters.name: ROM code
parameters.description: Each placed instance has a unique 64-bit ROM for multi-sensor bus tests.

tools.example: Two DS18B20 on one bus with an ATmega328P running the OneWire search; the Simulation Log flags timing violations if reset/presence pulses are too short.
tools.notes: 1-Wire timing is checked strictly; bit-banged drivers with wrong delays fail here before they fail on hardware.

tools.name: Analogue and I2C/SPI temperature sensors (LM35, LM20/LM34/LM45/LM50, TC72/TC74/TC77, MCP9800-MCP9803, MCP9600/9601)
tools.description: Temperature sensor models with an interactive temperature setting: analogue-output LM35 (10mV/C), LM20, LM34 (Fahrenheit), LM45, LM50; digital TC74 (I2C), TC72/TC77 (SPI), MCP9800-9803 (I2C, alert output) and the MCP9600/9601 thermocouple-to-digital converters. They feed ADC channels or serial buses so sensor-reading and calibration firmware can be tested against known values.
tools.usage: Pick Devices > 'LM35' > VOUT to an ADC pin; 'MCP9800' > SDA/SCL and ALERT; adjust temperature with the on-part arrows

parameters.name: Temperature
parameters.description: Interactive value (C) driving the output voltage or register.

tools.example: The Microchip F1 evaluation board sample reads an MCP9800 at address 0x90; the I2C analyser shows S 0x91 0x1B (27C) after a read request.
tools.notes: LM35 output is 10mV/C referenced to ground, so a 5V/10-bit ADC gives ~2 counts per degree - expect coarse readings unless a reference is used.

tools.name: Humidity sensors (DHT11, DHT22, SHT10/11/15, SHT21/25, SHT71/75, HTU21D, Si7021-A20, HYT271, TH02)
tools.description: Humidity/temperature sensor models: the single-wire DHT11 and DHT22 (AM2302) with their 40-bit frame and start-signal timing, Sensirion SHT1x (2-wire proprietary), SHT2x/HTU21D/Si7021 (I2C with hold/no-hold master modes and CRC), and the HYT271 and TH02 I2C sensors. Humidity and temperature are set interactively so DHT libraries, checksum handling and timing-critical bit-banging can be validated.
tools.usage: Pick Devices > 'DHT22' > DATA to the MCU pin with pull-up; 'SHT21' > SDA/SCL; set RH/T with the on-part controls

parameters.name: Humidity / Temperature
parameters.description: Interactive values encoded into the sensor's response frame.

tools.example: Uno + DHT22 (breakout in the Visual Designer gallery): readHumidity()/readTemperature() methods return the values set on the model; try 101% to check range handling.
tools.notes: The DHT single-wire protocol is timing sensitive - a wrong Processor Clock Frequency makes the checksum fail.

tools.name: Pressure sensors (BMP180, BMP280, MPL3115A2, MPX4115, MPX4250)
tools.description: Barometric/absolute pressure sensor models: Bosch BMP180 and BMP280 (I2C/SPI with calibration registers and compensation formulas), NXP MPL3115A2 (I2C altimeter/barometer) and the analogue-output Freescale MPX4115 and MPX4250. Pressure (and temperature for the digital parts) is adjusted interactively, and the digital parts return raw ADC values that the firmware must compensate exactly as with real silicon.
tools.usage: Pick Devices > 'BMP280' > SDA/SCL (or SPI), set pressure/temperature on the model; 'MPX4115' > VOUT to an ADC channel

parameters.name: Pressure
parameters.description: Interactive value in hPa/kPa.

tools.example: Pico W (MicroPython) + BMP280: read the raw registers, apply the datasheet compensation and print hPa; compare with the value set on the model.
tools.notes: The dsPIC33 Recorder tutorial uses the MPX4115 through an op-amp buffer into the ADC.

tools.name: Thermocouple, RTD and load-cell interfaces (MAX6674/MAX6675, MAX31855, MAX31856, MAX31865, AD594/AD595, RTD-PT100/PT1000, HX711)
tools.description: Instrumentation front-end models: MAX6675/MAX6674 and MAX31855 (K/J/N/S/T/E/R thermocouple types) SPI thermocouple-to-digital converters, MAX31856 universal thermocouple interface, MAX31865 RTD-to-digital with RTD-PT100/RTD-PT1000 sensor models, AD594/AD595 analogue thermocouple amplifiers and the HX711 24-bit load-cell ADC with its clock-pulse gain selection. Sensor temperature/force is set interactively.
tools.usage: Pick Devices > 'MAX31855K' > SCK/SO/CS to the MCU; 'HX711' > DOUT/PD_SCK; 'RTD-PT100' > MAX31865 input

parameters.name: Thermocouple type
parameters.description: Fixed by the part variant (MAX31855K, MAX31855T ...).

parameters.name: Gain (HX711)
parameters.description: Selected by the number of clock pulses after each conversion (25/26/27).

tools.example: Arduino + HX711: the HX711 library returns the value set on the load-cell model; step the clock-pulse loop with the logic analyser attached to PD_SCK/DOUT.
tools.notes: MAX6675 returns 12-bit values in 0.25C steps and flags an open thermocouple bit - test both branches of the firmware.

tools.name: Light sensors (TORCH_LDR, APDS-9002, ALS-PT19, GUR03)
tools.description: Light-dependent input models: TORCH_LDR (an LDR with an interactive torch whose distance sets the illuminance and hence the resistance), the APDS-9002 ambient-light photo sensor and ALS-PT19 phototransistor used by the Grove luminance modules, and GUR03. They are placed in a divider or transimpedance stage feeding an ADC to test nightlight, lux-measurement and threshold code.
tools.usage: Pick Devices > 'TORCH_LDR' > in a divider with a fixed resistor to an ADC pin; move the torch with the on-part arrows during simulation

parameters.name: Illuminance
parameters.description: Interactive torch distance (LDR) or lux value (APDS-9002, 0-1000 lux in the Grove model).

tools.example: Nightlight tutorial: Grove luminance sensor (APDS-9002) readLuminance() < 100 AND proximity < 20cm turns the Grove LED on.
tools.notes: Grove luminance and 80cm IR proximity modules are gallery peripherals built on these sensor models.

tools.name: Current sensors and power monitors (ACS712/ACS713/ACS755-ACS773, WCS1500, INA219, INA226, PAC1921)
tools.description: Hall-effect current sensor models (Allegro ACS712, ACS713, ACS755, ACS756, ACS758, ACS770, ACS772, ACS773 series and WCS1500) that output a voltage proportional to the current flowing through their sense path, and I2C power monitors (TI INA219, INA226 and Microchip PAC1921) that report bus voltage, shunt current and power in registers. Use them to test battery-monitoring, over-current and energy-metering firmware.
tools.usage: Pick Devices > 'ACS712ELCTR-05B' in series with the load, VOUT to an ADC pin; 'INA219' > VIN+/VIN- across a shunt, SDA/SCL to the MCU

parameters.name: Sensitivity
parameters.description: mV/A fixed by the ACS variant (185mV/A for 5A parts).

parameters.name: Calibration register (INA219)
parameters.description: Must be written by firmware to scale current/power readings.

tools.example: INA219 monitoring a DC motor: the Adafruit_INA219 library prints bus voltage and mA that match the DC Ammeter instrument in series.
tools.notes: ACS7xx outputs are ratiometric to VCC; a 3.3V ADC reading a 5V-powered sensor needs a divider, as on hardware.

tools.name: DC motors and encoders (MOTOR, MOTOR-DC with inertia, MOTOR-ENCODER, DC generator)
tools.description: Rotating machine models with animated shafts and RPM read-out: the simple MOTOR (ideal DC motor), the DC motor with inertia (acceleration follows the load/inertia properties), MOTOR-ENCODER (DC motor with quadrature encoder outputs for closed-loop speed/position firmware), the DC brushless model and a DC generator that produces voltage from mechanical drive. Winding resistance, back-EMF constant and inertia are properties, so PWM speed control and current-sense circuits behave realistically.
tools.usage: Pick Devices > 'MOTOR-ENCODER' > motor terminals to an H-bridge (L293D/L298/TB6612), encoder A/B outputs to interrupt pins

parameters.name: Nominal voltage / RPM
parameters.description: Sets the back-EMF constant.

parameters.name: Coil resistance / inductance
parameters.description: Electrical model for current-sense and driver testing.

parameters.name: Load inertia
parameters.description: Spin-up time; motors 'lose no momentum' while paused.

tools.example: PID speed loop on an ATmega328P: PWM to L298, encoder A/B on INT0/INT1; plot the set-point vs measured RPM with an analogue graph.
tools.notes: Because simulation time stops at breakpoints, motors hold their state while you step - a real advantage over hardware debugging.

tools.name: Stepper motors (MOTOR-STEPPER unipolar, MOTOR-BISTEPPER bipolar)
tools.description: Animated stepper motor models: the unipolar MOTOR-STEPPER (five/six leads, driven from a ULN2003/ULN2803 or transistor array) and the bipolar MOTOR-BISTEPPER (two coils, driven by an L293D/L298/DRV8825-class H-bridge or the L297/L298 pair). Full-step, half-step and microstep sequences turn the animated rotor and the model reports steps and direction, so sequencing firmware and the Arduino Stepper/AccelStepper libraries can be checked.
tools.usage: Pick Devices > 'MOTOR-STEPPER' > coil pins to ULN2003A outputs; 'MOTOR-BISTEPPER' > A+/A-/B+/B- to an H-bridge

parameters.name: Step angle
parameters.description: Degrees per full step (e.g. 1.8).

parameters.name: Coil resistance
parameters.description: Electrical load for driver testing.

tools.example: Arduino Motor Shield V1 R3 configured for one unipolar stepper (Visual Designer): setSpeed() then step(200) forward and step(-200) back; single-step the sequence and watch the rotor.
tools.notes: The Adafruit motor shield gallery entries come pre-populated with either DC motors or a stepper; the L297/L298 chipset models handle chopping and half-step generation.

tools.name: Servo, PWM servo, BLDC and 3-phase AC induction motors (MOTOR-SERVO, MOTOR-PWMSERVO, MOTOR-3PH)
tools.description: The remaining motor models: MOTOR-PWMSERVO (hobby RC servo whose angle follows the 1-2ms pulse on its signal pin, with the horn animated and angle displayed), MOTOR-SERVO (analogue servo with position feedback), the DC brushless (BLDC) motor with Hall/commutation outputs for six-step and FOC firmware, and the three-phase AC induction motor for inverter/VFD designs driven from IR2104/HIP4081A-class gate drivers.
tools.usage: Pick Devices > 'MOTOR-PWMSERVO' > signal pin to a PWM/timer output, V+/GND; 'MOTOR-3PH' > three phases from an inverter bridge

parameters.name: Pulse range
parameters.description: PWM servo maps 1ms-2ms (configurable) to -90..+90 degrees.

parameters.name: Poles / rated speed
parameters.description: BLDC and induction motor electrical parameters.

tools.example: PCA9685 + MOTOR-PWMSERVO on channel 0: writing 307 (1.5ms) centres the horn; Adafruit servo shield in the gallery does the same via setAngle().
tools.notes: Servo angle is printed on the model during simulation, which makes it a convenient visual PWM meter.

tools.name: Motor and gate drivers (L293D, L298, L297, L6201-L6203, DRV8816/8844/8871, TB6612FNG, IR2104, IR2184, HIP4080A/HIP4081A, LM5100/LM5101, ULN2003A/ULN2803A)
tools.description: Driver IC models placed between the MCU and motor models: quad half-H L293D, dual full-bridge L298 (and its L297 stepper controller companion), L6201-L6203 DMOS bridges, TI DRV8816/DRV8844/DRV8871, Toshiba TB6612FNG, the IR2104/IR2184 and HIP4080A/HIP4081A high-side/low-side MOSFET gate drivers with bootstrap behaviour, LM5100/LM5101 drivers and the ULN2003A/ULN2803A Darlington arrays with flyback diodes. They enforce enable/direction logic and dead-time so control firmware and bridge wiring errors are caught in simulation.
tools.usage: Pick Devices > 'L293D' > IN1/IN2/EN1 from the MCU, OUT1/OUT2 to a motor; 'IR2104' > IN/SD from PWM, HO/LO to a MOSFET half-bridge

parameters.name: Enable / standby pins
parameters.description: Must be driven correctly or outputs stay high-impedance (a common firmware oversight the model exposes).

tools.example: ULN2003A between PIC PORTB and MOTOR-STEPPER: an inverted coil sequence spins the rotor backwards - visible immediately.
tools.notes: Gate-driver models are analogue (SPICE) and need real MOSFET models on the bridge; use the Simulation Log if convergence problems appear with fast PWM edges.

tools.name: Relays and optocouplers (RELAY, 4N25-4N37, PC817, 6N136/6N137, H11AA1, CNY70, GK152)
tools.description: Electromechanical and opto-isolation models: the animated RELAY (SPDT/DPDT coil-driven switch with pull-in behaviour, plus vendor relay parts) for load-switching circuits, and optocouplers 4N25-4N37 and PC817 (phototransistor), 6N136/6N137 (high-speed logic output), H11AA1 (AC-input), the CNY70 reflective sensor and GK152 for isolated interfaces, zero-cross detection and line-following sensors.
tools.usage: Pick Devices > 'RELAY' > coil via a transistor/ULN2003A from the MCU, contacts in the load circuit with a flyback diode

parameters.name: Coil voltage / resistance
parameters.description: Relay pull-in threshold and drive current.

parameters.name: CTR (optocoupler)
parameters.description: Current transfer ratio of the SPICE model.

tools.example: Grove relay module (Visual Designer) switches a LAMP; the relay contact animates when on() is called.
tools.notes: Relay contacts are ideal switches; CNY70 is the sensor used for the Robot Turtle line-following simulation.

tools.name: I2C/SPI port expanders (MCP23008, MCP23009, MCP23016, MCP23017, MCP23S08, MCP23S09, MCP23S17)
tools.description: Microchip GPIO expander models with 8 or 16 bidirectional pins, configurable pull-ups, interrupt-on-change with mirrored INTA/INTB outputs and both I2C (MCP230xx) and SPI (MCP23Sxx) variants including hardware address pins. They are used for LCD/keypad backpacks and pin-count expansion and interact with the I2C/SPI analysers to verify register writes (IODIR, GPIO, GPPU, GPINTEN).
tools.usage: Pick Devices > 'MCP23017' > SDA/SCL, A0-A2 strapped, RESET high; GPA0-7/GPB0-7 to LEDs/switches

parameters.name: Address pins
parameters.description: A0-A2 select one of eight bus addresses (0x20-0x27).

tools.example: Arduino + MCP23017 driving 16 LEDs with Adafruit_MCP23017; enable INTA on a button and single-step the ISR.
tools.notes: The Getting Started schematic tutorial uses the MCP23008 with its datasheet download property configured.

tools.name: CAN bus models (MCP2515, MCP2518FD, MCP2551, MCP2561, MCP2562FD, TJA1050, SN65HVD230, vehicle ECU nodes)
tools.description: The CAN simulation set: MCP2515 (classical CAN 2.0B SPI controller with masks/filters, TX/RX buffers, interrupts) and MCP2518FD (CAN FD), transceivers MCP2551/MCP2561/MCP2562FD, TJA1050 and SN65HVD230, and over twenty behavioural 'car-part' nodes (Instrument Cluster, Engine ECU, Body Control Module, Vehicle Dynamics, Lighting Clusters ...) that generate and consume realistic frames. Together with the CAN Bus Analyser instrument they let automotive firmware be developed without a bench network.
tools.usage: Pick Devices > 'MCP2515' > SPI + INT to the MCU, TXCAN/RXCAN to an 'MCP2551' whose CANH/CANL join the bus with 120R terminators; add ECU node models and a CAN Bus Analyser

parameters.name: Bit rate
parameters.description: Set by firmware in the MCP2515 CNF registers; the analyser must be configured to match.

parameters.name: DBC file
parameters.description: Loaded into the analyser to decode frames by signal name.

tools.example: PIC18F4520 + MCP2515 + Engine ECU node: firmware requests RPM by ID, the analyser decodes the reply using the DBC and the Instrument Cluster node shows the gauge.
tools.notes: On-chip PIC18 ECAN is not modelled, so external MCP2515/2518FD controllers are the supported route. Fault injection (bit errors, bus-off) is available from the analyser.

tools.name: Ethernet controllers (ENC28J60, RTL8019AS)
tools.description: Network interface models that bridge the simulated MCU to the host PC's network stack: the Microchip ENC28J60 (SPI, 8KB buffer, MAC/MII registers) and the ISA/8-bit-bus Realtek RTL8019AS NE2000-compatible controller. Packets sent by the firmware (uIP, lwIP, EtherCard, Microchip TCP/IP stack) reach the real LAN and replies come back, so web-server, DHCP and MQTT firmware can be exercised end to end; Proteus 9.2 improved the wired Ethernet modelling for IoT work.
tools.usage: Pick Devices > 'ENC28J60' > SPI + INT/RESET to the MCU; configure the host network adapter binding in the part's properties

parameters.name: Host adapter
parameters.description: Physical NIC the model attaches to for real traffic.

parameters.name: MAC address
parameters.description: Set by firmware in the MAADR registers.

tools.example: ATmega328P + ENC28J60 running EtherCard's web server: browse to the simulated IP from the host and step the packet handler.
tools.notes: Real-network operation needs the Proteus network driver and a NIC that allows promiscuous binding; behaviour behind Wi-Fi adapters can be limited.

tools.name: COMPIM (physical COM port interface model)
tools.description: The Physical Interface Model for serial ports (ACTIVE.LIB): a DB9-style part whose TXD/RXD (and optional RTS/CTS/DTR/DSR) pins are connected to a real or virtual COM port on the host PC, so the simulated MCU's UART talks to external software - a terminal program, a GPS/GSM emulator, a PC application under development - or, through a virtual COM-port pair (com0com etc.), to another program. Baud rate, parity, data/stop bits and the physical/virtual baud can be set independently.
tools.usage: Pick Devices > 'COMPIM' > TXD/RXD to the MCU UART (crossed); Edit Component > Physical port COMx, Physical Baud Rate, Virtual Baud Rate, Data Bits, Parity, Stop Bits

parameters.name: Physical port
parameters.description: Host COM port (real or virtual pair).

parameters.name: Physical / Virtual Baud Rate
parameters.description: Can differ so a slow simulation still matches the external device rate.

parameters.name: Parity / Data / Stop bits
parameters.description: Frame format.

tools.example: Bluetooth or ESP8266 AT-command firmware: COMPIM on COM5 paired with COM6 where a PC script emulates the module's responses.
tools.notes: Use COMPIM (not the Virtual Terminal) whenever external software must be in the loop. Modem-control lines are optional; leave them unconnected if the firmware ignores handshaking.

tools.name: RS-232 / RS-485 transceivers (MAX220-MAX249 incl. MAX232, MAX487, MAX1480, DS275) and FT232 USB-serial bridge
tools.description: Level-converter and interface models: the MAX220-MAX249 RS-232 family (MAX232/MAX233 with charge pumps), MAX487 and MAX1480 RS-485 transceivers with driver/receiver enables for half-duplex multi-drop buses, the DS275 line-powered transceiver, and - from Proteus 9.0 - a fully supported FT232 USB-to-serial model (with I2C/SPI support) for boards that expose the MCU UART over USB.
tools.usage: Pick Devices > 'MAX232' > T1IN/R1OUT to the MCU UART, T1OUT/R1IN to a COMPIM or Virtual Terminal; 'MAX487' > DE/RE from the MCU for direction control

parameters.name: Direction control (RS-485)
parameters.description: DE/RE must be toggled by firmware; the model tri-states the bus otherwise.

tools.example: Two AVRs on a MAX487 RS-485 pair with a 120R terminator; step the master's DE assertion and watch the slave receive on the logic analyser.
tools.notes: The Virtual Terminal can be wired directly to MCU TTL pins; the transceiver models matter when checking inverted RS-232 levels or bus direction bugs.

tools.name: BLE and RFID simulation models
tools.description: Introduced in Proteus 9.2 as first-generation radio-protocol models: a Bluetooth Low Energy module model that exposes a serial/AT-style interface and advertises/connects to a simulated central, and an RFID reader/tag pair (MFRC522-class SPI reader with tag UIDs presented interactively). They let access-control, beacon and phone-connected firmware be developed without dedicated hardware.
tools.usage: Pick Devices > search 'BLE' / 'RFID' > wire UART or SPI to the MCU; present a tag or connect the central from the model's context controls during simulation

parameters.name: Tag UID / device name
parameters.description: Properties of the simulated tag or BLE peripheral.

tools.example: ESP32-S3 (MicroPython) + RFID reader: read a UID, compare with an allow-list and pulse a RELAY - all in simulation.
tools.notes: Described by Labcenter as first-generation models; check the 9.2 release notes for the supported command subset.

tools.name: ADC ICs (ADC0801-ADC0838, MCP3001/3202/3204/3208/3221/3301-3424, TLC548/549/1542/1543/2543, AD7321-AD7328, ADS1110, ADC128S102, LTC1860-LTC1865)
tools.description: External analogue-to-digital converter models spanning parallel (ADC0801-ADC0808/0809 with their START/EOC/ALE handshake, ADC0831-0838 serial), SPI (MCP3001/3202/3204/3208, TLC548/549, TLC1542/1543/2543, AD732x, ADC128S102, LTC186x) and I2C (MCP3221, MCP3421-3424 delta-sigma, ADS1110) parts. Conversion timing, reference inputs and result framing are modelled so driver code can be verified bit by bit with the SPI/I2C analysers.
tools.usage: Pick Devices > 'MCP3208' > CLK/DIN/DOUT/CS to the MCU SPI, CH0-CH7 from sensors/POT-HG, VREF to a reference

parameters.name: Reference voltage
parameters.description: VREF pin sets full scale; the model uses the actual node voltage.

parameters.name: Clock limits
parameters.description: Serial clock above the datasheet maximum is flagged in the Simulation Log.

tools.example: 8051 + ADC0804 in free-running mode: INTR drives INT0, the ISR reads the 8-bit bus and shows the value on a 7-segment pair.
tools.notes: Grove/breakout ADC modules in Visual Designer wrap these parts with read methods.

tools.name: DAC ICs (DAC0800/DAC0808/DAC0832, MCP4921/MCP4922/MCP4728/MCP4782, LTC1451/1456/1665/2440, MAX504-MAX522, AD5310/AD5320/AD5410/AD5420)
tools.description: Digital-to-analogue converter models: multiplying parallel DACs (DAC0800/0808 current-output, DAC0832 with double buffering), SPI DACs (MCP4921/4922 12-bit, MCP4782, LTC1451/1456, MAX504-MAX522, AD5310/AD5320), the I2C quad MCP4728 and 4-20mA loop DACs AD5410/AD5420. Output settles per the model so waveform-synthesis, calibration and industrial-loop firmware produce waveforms you can inspect on the oscilloscope or an analogue graph.
tools.usage: Pick Devices > 'MCP4921' > SCK/SDI/CS from the MCU, VREF to a reference, VOUT to the load; 'DAC0808' > D0-D7 from a port, IOUT to an op-amp I-V converter

parameters.name: Reference / gain bits
parameters.description: MCP49xx command bits (BUF, GA, SHDN) are decoded from the 16-bit word.

tools.example: PIC16F877A + DAC0808 + op-amp sine table: the analogue graph of VOUT shows the 64-step staircase sine.
tools.notes: Current-output DACs need the op-amp converter stage on the schematic just as on hardware.

tools.name: Op-amps, comparators and analogue signal-processing ICs (741, LM358, LM324, TL07x, LM339/LM393, AD8xxx, ADA45xx, INA125/INA132, LME497xx, LTC144x, THAT/VCA, RMS converters)
tools.description: SPICE-modelled analogue ICs: general-purpose op-amps (741, LM358/LM2904, LM324/LM2902, TL071-TL074, TLV27x), precision/instrumentation parts (AD8220-AD8228, AD8276/8277, INA125, INA132, MCP6N16), audio amplifiers (LM3875/3876/3886, LME49720/49721), high-speed AD8000/AD8129/AD8130, comparators LM339/LM393, LTC1440-LTC1442, LTC1540, MIC841/842, THAT2180/2181 VCAs and THAT2252/AD736/AD8436/LTC1966-1968 RMS-to-DC converters, plus the ideal OPAMP primitive for teaching. They run in both interactive and graph-based (frequency, noise, distortion) analyses.
tools.usage: Pick Devices > 'LM358' (or 'OPAMP' for the ideal primitive) > wire as usual; supply pins must be connected to power rails for the vendor models

parameters.name: Model source
parameters.description: Vendor SPICE subcircuit (SPICEMODEL) or Labcenter primitive; the picker's preview shows which.

parameters.name: Supply rails
parameters.description: Real models clip at the supply; the ideal OPAMP does not.

tools.example: Non-inverting LM358 gain-11 stage: Frequency graph from 10Hz-1MHz shows the gain-bandwidth roll-off; swap in the ideal OPAMP to see the difference.
tools.notes: Vendor models can cause convergence warnings at very fast edges - see the convergence troubleshooting entry. Comparators with open-collector outputs need pull-ups.

tools.name: 555/556 timers and oscillator ICs (NE555, NE556, TS556, LM566, LTC6903/LTC6904, AD537, AD9833)
tools.description: Timing and signal-source ICs: the NE555 (with the analogue-accurate model for astable/monostable circuits and threshold/trigger behaviour), dual NE556/TS556, the LM566 VCO, AD537 V-F converter, LTC6903/LTC6904 serially programmed oscillators and the AD9833 SPI DDS waveform generator. Use them for clock generation, PWM and frequency-synthesis experiments alongside microcontroller code.
tools.usage: Pick Devices > '555' or 'NE555' > RA/RB/C astable network; 'AD9833' > SPI from the MCU, VOUT to a filter

parameters.name: Timing components
parameters.description: External R/C values set the frequency; the model reproduces 1.1RC monostable and 0.693(RA+2RB)C astable timing.

tools.example: 555 astable at 1kHz clocking a 4017 decade counter driving ten LEDs - a classic first digital simulation.
tools.notes: The 555 is an analogue model, so a Digital graph on its output still requires the mixed-mode simulator; use an Analogue graph for the capacitor waveform.

tools.name: Logic families (74STD/74LS/74ALS/74AS/74F/74S/74HC/74HCT and CMOS 4000 series)
tools.description: The digital IC libraries: every common TTL sub-family (74, 74LS, 74ALS, 74AS, 74F, 74S) and CMOS 74HC/74HCT parts, plus the 4000-series CMOS library (4001, 4011, 4017, 4026, 4047, 4051, 4060, 4511, ...). Each part is a DSIM digital model with family-specific propagation delays, so timing hazards, glitches and fan-out issues can be seen on a Digital graph or the Logic Analyser, and they interoperate with analogue parts through the mixed-mode interface (ITFMOD) automatically.
tools.usage: Pick Devices > category 'TTL 74LS series' / 'CMOS 4000 series' > e.g. '74LS138', '4017'; VCC/GND are implicit power pins

parameters.name: Family timing
parameters.description: Typical/min/max delay selection is controlled by the digital simulator options (DSIM).

tools.example: 74HC595 shift register driven by an AVR SPI bus into eight LEDs: single-step the latch pulse and see the outputs update.
tools.notes: Hidden power pins connect to VCC/GND nets defined in Configure Power Rails; if a chip is dead, check the rail voltage there. Logic thresholds differ between HC (CMOS) and LS (TTL) models.

tools.name: Voltage regulators, supervisors and references (78xx/79xx, LM1117/LD1117/LM1086/LM2940, LT3010, LMR62014, ADM705-ADM708, MCP809/MCP810, TLC77xx, LM385, LM4041, AD58x/AD680/AD780, MAX873-MAX876)
tools.description: Power-management models: linear regulators 78xx/78Lxx and 79xx/79Lxx, LF series, LM1086, LD1117/LM1117 (LDO 3.3V/adjustable), LM2940, LT3010 and the LMR62014 boost converter; supervisory/reset ICs ADM705-ADM708, MCP809/MCP810 and TLC7701/7703/7705/7725/7733 with reset timing and watchdog inputs; and precision references LM385, LM4041, AD581/AD584/AD587, AD680, AD780, MAX873-MAX876 and MAX1044. They let the power section of a board be simulated with real dropout and reset behaviour rather than an ideal DC source.
tools.usage: Pick Devices > '7805' > IN from a DC source, OUT to the circuit with decoupling capacitors; 'MCP809' > VDD monitored rail, RESET to the MCU MCLR

parameters.name: Dropout / load regulation
parameters.description: Modelled by the SPICE subcircuit; check the output on a DC voltmeter under load.

tools.example: Battery-powered design: sweep the input from 9V to 6V with a DC Sweep graph and see where the 7805 output drops out and the MCP809 asserts reset.
tools.notes: LM317-style adjustable regulators are found under the analogue ICs library; for quick tests the POWER/GROUND terminals with Configure Power Rails avoid regulators entirely.

tools.name: Discrete and passive primitives (RES, CAP, INDUCTOR, DIODE, BJT, MOSFET, JFET, TRAN-2P2S transformers, CRYSTAL, FUSE)
tools.description: The SPICE primitive libraries behind every analogue simulation: resistors (RES, CHIPRES, RESPACK), capacitors (CAP, CAP-ELEC), inductors, diodes/zeners/LEDs from the DIODE library, bipolar transistors (NPN/PNP generic plus vendor 2N/BC/TIP parts), MOSFETs (IRF/2N7000/generic NMOS/PMOS with level 1-3 models), JFETs, transformers TRAN-2P2S/TRAN-2P3S (turns ratio, coupling, primary inductance), CRYSTAL (for schematic completeness - MCU timing comes from the clock property), FUSE and the ideal SWITCH primitives. Values accept SI suffixes and tolerance/temperature properties where the model supports them.
tools.usage: Pick Devices > 'RES' then set Value = 4k7; 'TRAN-2P2S' > set Primary Inductance and Turns Ratio properties; 'IRF540' etc. for vendor MOSFETs

parameters.name: Value
parameters.description: Component value with SI suffix (1k, 100n, 10u).

parameters.name: PRIMITIVE / SPICEMODEL
parameters.description: Hidden properties selecting the SPICE model type or vendor subcircuit.

parameters.name: Transformer parameters
parameters.description: Primary inductance, secondary inductance or turns ratio, coupling factor.

tools.example: Bridge rectifier + 1000u smoothing capacitor from a TRAN-2P2S (230V:12V): Analogue graph of the output shows ripple; add a 7805 for a complete PSU.
tools.notes: Parts with no model (schematic-only symbols) are flagged in the picker preview; 'Show only parts with models' filters them out. Unconnected inductors/transformer windings and floating nodes are the most common cause of convergence failures.
